title: Clean Hands, Clean Hearts, and a Mother from Tyre
sum: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see some of Jesus' disciples eating without the ritual hand-washing that the tradition of the elders required. Mark stops to explain the custom for readers who do not know it. Jesus answers with Isaiah's charge of lip-service and with a case where a tradition, the Korban vow, cancels God's command to honor parents. Then he tells the crowd a riddle: nothing that goes into a person from outside makes him unclean; what comes out of him does. Indoors he explains it to the disciples, and Mark adds that with this he made all foods clean.

Jesus goes into Gentile territory near Tyre, hoping to stay hidden. A Greek woman, Syrophoenician by birth, begs him to free her daughter from a demon. He answers that the children must eat first and their bread should not go to the little dogs; she answers that the little dogs eat the children's scraps, and her daughter is set free. Coming back by a long route through Sidon and the Ten Cities, Jesus heals a deaf man who can barely speak, with fingers, spit, a groan and an Aramaic word: "Ephphatha." The crowd cries that he does everything well.
readings: Read as a debate within Judaism

Jesus argues as a Jewish teacher, setting the written command to honor parents above an oral rule and the purity of the heart above the purity of hands. Jewish scholars such as Daniel Boyarin and Yair Furstenberg read the riddle of 7:15 as a defense of the Torah's own purity system against a newer Pharisaic idea, not as an attack on the food laws. On this reading Mark's comment in 7:19 is the Gospel writer's application for his own Gentile church.
Read as the opening of the door to the nations

The chapter moves from a dispute about the purity that separated Jews from Gentiles, through a Gentile mother's wise answer, to healings in Gentile land. Mark's comment that Jesus "made all foods clean" removes the main barrier at the table between Jewish and Gentile believers, the barrier that troubled the early church (Acts 10–11; Galatians 2:11–14). The bread for the children overflows to the little dogs, and in chapter 8 a mostly Gentile crowd is fed.

views.H: Hand-washing before ordinary meals was a Pharisaic practice, not a law of Moses; the Mishnah later gives it a whole tractate (Yadayim). How widely it was kept in Jesus' day is debated: E. P. Sanders thought it a pious minority practice. The Korban formula is found on a Jerusalem ossuary lid, and Mishnah Nedarim 9:1 lets such a vow be released when it harms parents. Tyre was a rich Gentile port that bought Galilean grain; the Decapolis was a league of Greek cities east of the lake.
views.C: Matthew 15 follows Mark closely but drops Mark's explanation of Jewish customs (7:3–4), his comment "he made all foods clean" (7:19) and his healing of the deaf man (7:31–37), which Luke also omits. Many scholars take these as signs that Mark is earlier and wrote for Gentiles, and that Matthew, writing for Jewish believers, softened the food-law point. The Latin loanword for "jugs" (7:4) and the term "Syrophoenician" (7:26) fit the tradition that Mark wrote in Rome.
views.L: The chapter turns on inside and outside: food that goes into the body, evil that comes out of the heart; a Gentile woman outside Israel who speaks wisely while insiders misunderstand (7:18). Jesus' riddle in public and explanation in private repeat the pattern of chapter 4. The deaf man whose ears are opened (7:31–37) and the blind man healed in stages (8:22–26) frame a section in which the disciples are deaf and blind to what the bread means (8:18).
views.J: The opponents are fellow Jews, and the question is how to keep God's law faithfully, a debate Jews still hold. Jesus quotes Isaiah and the Ten Words against a tradition, as later rabbis did when they released harmful vows. Mark's "all the Jews" (7:3) is an outsider's simplification, and the passage has often been read as if Jesus rejected Judaism; Jewish and Christian scholars today stress that it is an argument within it.
views.T: Christians have long read 7:19 as freeing believers from the food laws, citing it with Acts 10 and Romans 14 (the Catechism of the Catholic Church 582 cites Mark 7:18–21). The Syrophoenician woman became a model of humble, persistent prayer. The "Ephphatha" of 7:34 entered the baptismal rite as early as Ambrose of Milan, and the Catholic rite still includes an optional Ephphatha prayer over the newly baptized.

deep.b:
The chapter begins with hands and ends with foods, and readers have often run the two together. The question in 7:5 is about ritual hand-washing, a tradition of the elders. The riddle in 7:15 is about what can make a person unclean. Mark's comment in 7:19 applies the riddle to "all foods."

The common Christian reading takes Jesus to declare the whole system of clean and unclean food obsolete, and Mark to say so for his Gentile readers (Marcus, Collins, France). A Jewish-historical reading (Furstenberg, Boyarin) sees Jesus defending the older biblical view, in which impurity does not pass into a person through what he eats, against a Pharisaic novelty that made unwashed hands defile the food and so the eater; Mark's comment would then be his own extension, or, in Boyarin's reading, a remark about digestion. A middle view (Rudolph) holds that 7:19 concerns food made impure by contact, not the kinds of animals Leviticus forbids.

What all agree on is the center of the passage: "What leaves a person, that is the thing that makes a person unclean" (7:20). The heart, not the hand, is where defilement starts. On how the churches apply this today, see the food-laws card at Matthew 15.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the scraps and the seven baskets
deep.b: The Syrophoenician woman asks only for the "scraps" (psichia) that fall from the children's table (7:28). In the very next meal, in Gentile country, the leftover pieces fill seven large hampers (8:8), more than the twelve small baskets left after the Jewish crowd was fed (6:43). I suspect Mark wants readers to set the two side by side: what the mother hoped would be crumbs turns out to be a surplus. The words differ (psichia and klasmata), so this is a link of story, not of vocabulary, and commentators who read the second feeding as a Gentile meal (for example Marcus) make a similar connection in general terms.

echoes: Isaiah 29:13; Exodus 20:12; Exodus 21:17; Deuteronomy 5:16; Leviticus 11:1–47; Numbers 30:2; Isaiah 35:5–6; Genesis 1:31; 1 Kings 17:8–24; Matthew 15:1–31; Luke 11:37–41; Acts 10:9–16; Romans 14:14; Galatians 2:11–14

settings.what: Jesus' answer about tradition and the Korban vow
settings.to: The Pharisees and the scribes who had come from Jerusalem
settings.when: In Galilee, after they object that his disciples eat with unwashed hands
settings.why: To turn their question back on them. The rule at stake is a Pharisaic tradition, hand-washing before meals, which bound those who accepted the tradition of the elders, not a law of Moses. Jesus answers with another of their rulings: a vow that dedicates property as Korban could keep a son from supporting his parents, so that a human rule cancels the fifth commandment. Isaiah's words name the deeper fault, honor from the lips with the heart far away. Matthew 15:1–9 puts the Korban charge before the Isaiah quotation; Luke has no parallel.
settings.readers: Mark's first readers, most likely Gentile believers in Rome in the 60s (some scholars place them in Syria or Galilee; see the book's introduction), needed Mark's explanation of the customs (7:3–4). They learned that the question was not whether Jews were wrong to be careful but whether any tradition may override God's command.

settings.what: The riddle about what makes a person unclean
settings.to: The crowd, called back to listen
settings.when: Right after the dispute with the Jerusalem visitors
settings.why: To give everyone, not only the experts, a saying to puzzle over: impurity does not come from what enters a person but from what comes out. It is a mashal, a riddle, meant to make hearers think, and it does: even the disciples need it explained. Matthew 15:10–11 has the same setting but speaks of what enters and leaves "the mouth."
settings.readers: Mark's readers heard in it the basis for Jewish and Gentile believers eating together.
views: Read with 7:19, the saying abolishes the distinction between clean and unclean foods for Jesus' followers.
The saying ranks moral impurity above ritual impurity, in the prophets' manner, without cancelling the Torah's laws (Vermes, Dunn).
The saying defends the biblical view that impurity does not pass into the body through food (Furstenberg).

settings.to: His disciples, indoors, away from the crowd
settings.when: When they ask him about the riddle
settings.why: To make plain what the riddle meant: food passes through the belly, while the heart is the source of evil plans and deeds. The list of twelve vices turns the disciples from the question of other people's hands to their own hearts. In Matthew 15:12–20 Peter asks the question, the comment on foods is absent, and the answer ends with hand-washing (Matthew 15:20).
settings.readers: Mark gives his readers his own comment, "With this he made all foods clean," as the teaching's meaning for their mixed churches.

settings.what: The conversation with the Syrophoenician woman
settings.by: Jesus and a Greek woman of Syrophoenician birth
settings.to: Each other, in a house near Tyre
settings.when: When she throws herself at his feet and begs him to free her daughter
settings.why: Her aim is clear: help for her daughter. Jesus' saying about the children and the little dogs states the order of his mission, Israel first. She accepts the order and finds room in it for herself, and he grants her request because of her answer. In Matthew 15:21–28 she is "a Canaanite woman" who first meets silence; the disciples ask Jesus to send her away, and he says he was sent only to Israel's lost sheep. Luke has no parallel.
settings.readers: Readers who were mostly Gentiles saw a Gentile mother receive what she asked for, not by denying Israel's place but by trusting the bread was enough for the little dogs too.
views: Jesus intended to help and drew out her persistence and faith (Chrysostom and many others).
Sharon Ringe and many other modern and feminist interpreters think the woman truly changed Jesus' mind and widened his mission.
The saying is about order, not contempt: "first" leaves room for the nations (Romans 1:16).

settings.to: A deaf man who struggled to speak, taken aside from the crowd
settings.when: In the Decapolis, after touching his ears and tongue
settings.why: To open the man's ears with a word he could not hear but could see spoken, after Jesus has explained in signs what he was about to do. Mark keeps the Aramaic so that his Greek readers hear Jesus' own voice. Matthew 15:29–31 has a summary of many healings on a mountain instead of this one.
settings.readers: Some of Mark's readers may already have heard "Ephphatha" at their own baptisms, as later churches did.

settings.when: After the deaf man is healed
settings.why: Their praise, "He makes the deaf able to hear and the speechless able to speak," echoes Isaiah 35:5–6 and the creation story's "very good." Gentiles unknowingly announce that the age Isaiah promised has begun.
settings.readers: Gentile readers heard Gentiles praising the God of Israel's promised salvation, as they themselves did.

title: Bread, Blindness and the Road to the Cross
sum: A second large crowd, probably mostly Gentile, has been with Jesus three days, and he feeds four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish. The Pharisees demand a sign from heaven; Jesus refuses with an oath. In the boat, with one loaf, he warns the disciples against the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod, and they think he is talking about bread. He asks them a string of questions: Are your hearts hardened? Don't you remember the baskets? Don't you understand yet?

At Bethsaida Jesus heals a blind man in two stages: first he sees people like walking trees, then everything clearly. Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who people say he is, and Peter answers, "You are the Messiah." Jesus then teaches openly that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise after three days. Peter rebukes him; Jesus rebukes Peter as Satan. Then he calls the crowd and his disciples to say no to themselves, take up their cross and follow him, because whoever loses his life for him and the good news will save it.
readings: Many historians think the scene at Caesarea Philippi preserves a real turning point: Jesus' followers saw him as Messiah, and Jesus, knowing John's fate and the Romans' habits, warned them that suffering lay ahead. How much of the predictions' detail goes back to Jesus and how much was shaped after Easter is debated.

The chapter is a hinge. The section on bread (6:30–8:21) ends with the disciples blind to what the loaves mean; a blind man is healed in two stages; Peter sees half the truth, that Jesus is Messiah, but not the other half, that he must suffer. From here the road leads to Jerusalem, and the way of the Messiah becomes the way of the disciple.

views.H: The second feeding takes place in or near the Decapolis. Bethsaida, rebuilt by Herod Philip, and Caesarea Philippi, his capital at the source of the Jordan with its shrine of Pan and temple to Augustus, lay in Philip's territory, outside Antipas' reach. Josephus tells of men who promised signs to their followers and were destroyed by Rome, the background for the demand in 8:11. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for rebels and slaves; "pick up his cross" meant walking to execution.
views.C: Mark's confession is the shortest: "You are the Messiah" (8:29). Matthew 16 adds "the Son of the living God" and Jesus' blessing of Peter; Luke 9 has "God's Messiah" and omits Peter's rebuke. Luke also omits the whole stretch from Mark 6:45 to 8:26, including the second feeding and the blind man of Bethsaida, which scholars call Luke's "great omission." Matthew and Luke both drop the two-stage healing. Mark's "after three days" becomes "on the third day" in both.
views.L: Mark builds 8:22–10:52 as one section on the road to Jerusalem, framed by two blind men and built on three passion predictions (see "Two blind men frame the road" below). The triple "rebuke" in 8:30–33 makes the confession a contest between two ideas of the Messiah.
views.J: "Messiah" meant different things to different Jews: a royal son of David who would defeat Israel's enemies (Psalms of Solomon 17), a priestly figure, or a heavenly judge. A suffering Messiah was not a common expectation, though the suffering righteous one and the servant of Isaiah 53 were known texts. Peter's protest is a reasonable Jewish response; Jesus' reply joins the Messiah to Daniel's Son of Man and to suffering.
views.T: Church fathers took the seven baskets as the Gentile church and the second feeding as a sign of the Eucharist. Peter's confession, together with Matthew's fuller version, became central to Christian teaching on Christ and, in Matthew, on Peter's office (see the card at Matthew 16:18). The call to take up the cross shaped the theology of martyrdom and, later, of self-denial in monastic and Protestant piety alike.

deep.h: Two blind men frame the road
deep.b:
Mark sets his central section between two healings of blind men. At Bethsaida (8:22–26) the healing takes two touches: first the man sees people "as trees, walking around," then everything clearly. At Jericho (10:46–52) Bartimaeus sees at once and follows Jesus "on the way." Between them Jesus walks toward Jerusalem with disciples who see only in part.

PredictionMisunderstandingTeaching
8:31Peter rebukes Jesus (8:32–33)Take up your cross (8:34–9:1)
9:31They argue who ranks highest (9:33–34)First must be last, servant of all (9:35–37)
10:33–34James and John ask for the best seats (10:35–40)The Son of Man came to serve and give his life (10:42–45)

Most commentators, of many schools, recognize this design. It means that Peter's confession is not the end of the disciples' blindness but the first touch. Mark's readers, who knew the confession by heart, were being asked whether they had received the second.

The road itself carries the theme. Hodos means both "road" and "way." Mark opened with Isaiah's call to get the Lord's road ready (1:2–3); from Caesarea Philippi on, Jesus and the disciples are always "on the road" (8:27; 9:33–34; 10:17; 10:32), and the section ends with Bartimaeus following him "on the road" (10:52). Early Christians called their faith "the Way" (Acts 9:2; Acts 24:14), so Mark's readers could hear their own name for discipleship in this road: it leads to Jerusalem and a cross, and following Jesus means walking it with him. Chapter 10 brings the teaching to its key, the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life (10:45; see the chapter page for Mark 10).

From 6:30 to 8:21, bread runs through every scene: five thousand fed (6:30–44), disciples who had not grasped what the loaves meant (6:52), hands washed before bread (7:2), the children's bread and the dogs' scraps (7:27–28), four thousand fed (8:1–9), one loaf in the boat and the yeast (8:14–21). The section ends with a question, not an answer: "Don't you understand yet?" (8:21). Many readers take the answer to be that the bread Jesus gives is for Jew and Gentile alike, and that the one who gives it is in the boat with them.

echoes: Exodus 16:1–36; 2 Kings 4:42–44; Psalm 118:22; Jeremiah 5:21; Ezekiel 12:2; Isaiah 6:9–10; Isaiah 53:3–12; Daniel 7:13–14; Psalm 2:2; Matthew 15:32–39; Matthew 16:1–28; Luke 9:18–27; John 6:66–69

settings.what: Jesus' compassion for the four thousand
settings.when: After three days with a large crowd, probably in or near the Decapolis
settings.why: To draw the disciples into his concern for hungry people far from home and to see again what God can do with little. Their answer, "Where could anyone get bread?", shows they have not learned from the first feeding.
settings.readers: Readers who had come to faith "from far off" could see themselves in the crowd fed at Jesus' table.

settings.to: Pharisees who came out to dispute with him
settings.when: After the second feeding, probably on the west side of the lake (8:10, 13)
settings.why: To refuse proof on demand. With a Hebrew oath form, Jesus says no sign will be given to a generation that asks in order to test him. His acts of power were not meant to compel belief. Matthew tells the demand twice, and both times Jesus promises "the sign of Jonah" (Matthew 12:38–39; Matthew 16:1–4); Luke 11:29 has the saying spoken to the crowds. Mark's "no sign at all" is the starkest form.
settings.readers: A church with no wonders to show its accusers learned that faith does not rest on signs produced to order.

settings.what: The warning about yeast and the questions about bread
settings.when: Crossing the lake, with only one loaf on board
settings.why: To warn them against the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and of Herod, and, when they think only of bread, to wake them up. His questions repeat the prophets' words about blind eyes and deaf ears and ask them to remember the baskets. Matthew 16:6–12 names "the Pharisees and Sadducees" and explains the yeast as their teaching; Luke 12:1 sets the warning before a crowd of thousands and calls the yeast hypocrisy.
settings.readers: The question "Don't you understand yet?" is put to the reader too, who is invited to see who was in the boat with them.

settings.to: The disciples, on the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi
settings.when: At the turning point of the Gospel, before the journey to Jerusalem
settings.why: To move the disciples from what others say to what they themselves believe. Peter names Jesus the Messiah; Jesus then orders silence, because the title will be misunderstood until he has taught what kind of Messiah he is. Luke 9:18 sets the question after Jesus has been praying alone, and names no place.
settings.readers: Readers who confessed the same words at baptism are shown that the confession is true but incomplete without the cross.

settings.what: The first prediction of the passion and the rebuke of Peter
settings.to: The disciples, and Peter in particular
settings.why: To teach openly that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the council, be killed and rise. When Peter objects, Jesus treats the objection as Satan's temptation and sends Peter back to a follower's place. Luke 9:22 has the prediction but no rebuke of Peter.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Peter as an apostle, and by tradition as a martyr in Rome, saw that even he had to learn this lesson.

settings.what: The call to take up the cross
settings.to: The crowd together with his disciples
settings.why: To make the way of the Messiah the way of all who follow him: saying no to oneself, carrying a cross, losing one's life for him and the good news. The sayings end with the Son of Man's coming in glory and a promise that some will see the kingdom arrive in power. Matthew 16:24 has the call spoken to the disciples only, Luke 9:23 "to all." Matthew 10:38 and Luke 14:27 give the cross saying in other settings: the sending of the Twelve, and the crowds traveling with Jesus.
settings.readers: If, as most think, Mark's readers were in Rome, they had seen fellow believers crucified and burned under Nero (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), and heard this as a word about faithfulness under trial and about shame before the Son of Man.

title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure Below
sum: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and he is transfigured: his clothes become whiter than any fuller could make them. Elijah and Moses appear and talk with him. Peter, terrified, offers to build three booths, and a voice from the cloud says, "This is my dearly loved Son. Listen to him!" Coming down, Jesus orders silence until the Son of Man rises from the dead and explains that Elijah has already come and suffered, as the Son of Man must.

Below, the other disciples have failed to free a boy from a spirit that throws him into fire and water. His father begs, "If there is anything you are able to do," and Jesus answers that anything is possible for the one who believes. "I believe! Help me with my unbelief!" Jesus frees the boy and lifts him up. Back in Galilee Jesus predicts his death a second time; the disciples do not understand and argue about who ranks highest. Jesus sets a child in their midst, tells John not to stop an outsider who casts out demons in his name, and warns, in hard sayings about Gehenna, fire and salt, against tripping up the little ones.
readings: Read as a vision of glory before the cross

The transfiguration gives the three disciples, and Mark's readers, a glimpse of who Jesus is before the darkness of the passion. The voice confirms Peter's confession and corrects his objection: this Son must be heard when he speaks of suffering. Most church fathers also saw in it the promise of 9:1 fulfilled.
Read as a story of failing disciples

The chapter's second half shows disciples who cannot cast out a spirit, cannot understand the prediction, argue about rank and try to stop an outsider. Mark sets the glory of the mountain beside the failure below, and Jesus' answer each time is prayer, service, welcome to the least and the cutting away of whatever trips others up.

views.H: The mountain is unnamed; tradition since the 300s names Mount Tabor in Galilee, while many modern scholars prefer Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, or a height nearby. Jewish expectation of Elijah's return before the end rests on Malachi 4:5–6 and appears in Sirach 48:10 and the Mishnah. The boy's symptoms resemble epilepsy, which Matthew calls being "moonstruck." Rank and precedence mattered in every ancient group, including the Qumran community.
views.C: Mark's account is the earliest and roughest: Peter calls Jesus "Rabbi," is terrified and does not know what to say; Matthew and Luke soften these details. Mark alone has the father's cry "Help me with my unbelief!" and Jesus taking the child in his arms. "And fasting" in 9:29 and the repeated refrain in 9:44 and 9:46 are later additions to the text. The sayings of 9:37–50 seem gathered by catchwords; Matthew and Luke place several of them elsewhere.
views.L: The chapter mirrors Moses on Sinai: six days, a mountain, a cloud, a voice, a shining figure, and a descent to faithless people below (Exodus 24; 32; 34). The resurrection theme runs from the mountain (9:9–10) to the boy who lies "like a dead body" and is "raised" and "rises" (9:26–27). The second prediction (9:31) is followed, as in the pattern of 8:31–10:45, by misunderstanding (9:33–34) and teaching about service (9:35–37).
views.J: Elijah and Moses were the two great figures of Israel's hope: the prophet who would return and the lawgiver whose like God would raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15). The disciples' question about Elijah is a scribal question, reasonably asked, and Jesus answers with the Scriptures. The outsider who uses Jesus' name recalls Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp (Numbers 11:26–29). Isaiah 66:24, behind 9:48, was read by Jews of the time as a picture of final judgment.
views.T: The Feast of the Transfiguration (August 6) is one of the twelve great feasts of the Orthodox Church and is kept by Catholics, Anglicans and Lutherans; the Orthodox tradition sees in the light of Tabor the uncreated glory of God (see the card). The father's cry has become a prayer for doubting believers. "Prayer and fasting" (9:29, in the longer text) shaped the church's practice of fasting before exorcism and baptism. The sayings about Gehenna have been central to the doctrine of hell.

deep.b:
Mark's account is the shortest and most unpolished of the three. He describes only the clothes, not the face; he names Elijah before Moses; Peter calls Jesus "Rabbi" and speaks out of terror. Matthew 17 adds the shining face and the disciples falling on their faces; Luke 9:28–36 says the three talked with Jesus about his "departure" at Jerusalem, and that the disciples were heavy with sleep. 2 Peter 1:16–18 remembers the voice on "the holy mountain" as proof that the apostles did not follow made-up stories.

In Mark the scene answers chapter 8. Peter has called Jesus Messiah and refused the cross; now God calls him Son and says, "Listen to him." The glory is real, but it is shown on the way to suffering, and the disciples must keep silent about it until the resurrection (9:9). See the deep dive on the transfiguration and Sinai at Matthew 17.

The views on 9:1 are set out in the note on the verse. What tests each of them is that Mark has three sayings about the time, and they seem to pull apart: some standing here will see the kingdom arrive in power (9:1); this generation will not pass away before all these things happen (13:30); no one knows that day or hour, not even the Son (13:32).

Readers who see the transfiguration in 9:1 separate the three: 9:1 is fulfilled a week later, 13:30 refers to the events of 13:5–23, and 13:32 to the final day. Readers who see AD 70 join 9:1 and 13:30 as the temple's fall within that generation, and keep 13:32 for the end. Readers who see the resurrection and Pentecost read "in power" as Paul does of the risen Son (Romans 1:4). Albert Schweitzer and many critical scholars read all three as one expectation: Jesus denied knowing the day, not the generation. Mark sets 9:1 directly before the mountain, which suggests how he wanted it heard first.

deep.title: Claude's theory: exorcism turned inward
deep.b: Mark's word for what to do with an eye that trips you up is ekbale, "throw it out" (9:47), the verb he uses throughout the Gospel for throwing out demons, and three times in this chapter for the spirit the disciples could not expel (9:18, 28) and the outsider who could (9:38). I suspect Mark means the echo: disciples who failed to throw out a spirit, and who wanted to stop someone who succeeded, are told what they must throw out of their own lives. Prayer (9:29) and self-discipline (9:43–47) answer the same failure. I have not seen this link drawn in the commentaries I know, though the catchword structure of 9:37–50 is widely noted.

echoes: Exodus 24:12–18; Exodus 34:29–35; 1 Kings 19:8–18; Malachi 4:4–6; Deuteronomy 18:15; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 53:3; Numbers 11:26–29; Isaiah 66:24; Leviticus 2:13; Matthew 17:1–23; Matthew 18:1–9; Luke 9:28–50; 2 Peter 1:16–18

settings.to: Peter, James and John, on the mountain
settings.when: As Peter offers to build three booths
settings.why: To name Jesus as God's dearly loved Son before the three witnesses and to command them to listen to him, above all to what he has just said about suffering (8:31–38). At the baptism the voice spoke to Jesus; here it speaks about him to his followers.
settings.readers: Mark's readers heard God's own verdict on the one they confessed, set within a story that would end at a cross.

settings.what: The order to keep silent and the question about Elijah
settings.to: Peter, James and John, coming down the mountain
settings.why: To set a time limit on silence, until the Son of Man rises, and to answer a scribal objection: if Elijah must come first, how can the end be near? Jesus agrees that Elijah comes first, says he has come and suffered (John the Baptist), and insists that the Son of Man too must suffer. Matthew 17:13 adds that the disciples understood he meant John the Baptist; Luke has no parallel.
settings.readers: Readers who now proclaimed the glory openly learned why it had stayed hidden until Easter, and that the forerunner had died before the Messiah did.

settings.what: The words around the boy's healing
settings.by: Jesus, the boy's father, and the disciples
settings.to: The crowd and scribes, the father, the spirit, and finally the disciples in private
settings.when: At the foot of the mountain, after the disciples have failed
settings.why: Jesus' lament over a faithless generation, his answer to the father ("anything is possible for the one who believes"), his command to the spirit and his private word to the disciples ("except prayer") all press one point: power over evil comes from trust in God, not from a technique the disciples possess. Matthew 17:20 gives the disciples a different answer: their little faith, and faith like a mustard seed. Luke 17:6 has the mustard-seed saying in another setting.
settings.readers: Readers who knew failure and mixed faith could pray the father's words: "I believe! Help me with my unbelief!"

settings.what: The second prediction of the passion
settings.to: His disciples, traveling secretly through Galilee
settings.when: On the way from the mountain to Capernaum
settings.why: To teach them again, in a short and sharp form, that the Son of Man is being handed over and will be killed and rise. They do not understand and are afraid to ask.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that Jesus had been "handed over" knew too that some of them might be handed over (13:9–12).

settings.what: First and last, and the child in their midst
settings.to: The Twelve, in a house in Capernaum
settings.when: After they argued on the road about who ranked highest
settings.why: To reverse their idea of greatness: the first must be last and servant of all, and welcoming a child, the person of no rank, is welcoming Jesus and the God who sent him. In Matthew 18:1–5 the disciples ask Jesus who is greatest; Luke 9:46–48 tells of their argument. The saying about first and last returns elsewhere (10:43–44; Matthew 23:11; Luke 22:26, at the Last Supper).
settings.readers: Leaders of house churches among Mark's readers learned that rank in Jesus' community is measured by service to the least.

settings.what: The outsider who cast out demons
settings.when: When John reports that they tried to stop a man using Jesus' name
settings.why: To stop the disciples from guarding Jesus' name as their own possession. Anyone doing good in his name is not an enemy, and even a cup of water given to his people will be rewarded. Luke 9:49–50 keeps the scene. Matthew has no such scene; its cup-of-water saying stands in the sending of the Twelve (Matthew 10:42).
settings.readers: Readers who met other groups using Jesus' name heard Jesus counsel generosity, not rivalry.
views: The saying teaches openness to Christians outside one's own circle.
It concerns those who act in Jesus' name, not anyone who is merely neutral; elsewhere "anyone who is not on my side is against me" (Matthew 12:30).

settings.what: The warnings about snares, Gehenna and salt
settings.to: The Twelve, in the house at Capernaum
settings.when: Continuing the teaching after the child and the outsider
settings.why: To warn disciples who argue about rank and exclude others that tripping up a humble believer is worse than drowning, and that anything in their own lives that leads to sin must be cut away whatever the cost. The section ends with salt: be a covenant people, and keep peace with one another. Matthew 18:6–9 keeps the snares in the same setting, but Matthew 5:29–30 also puts the eye and the hand in the Sermon on the Mount, about lust. The salt sayings stand elsewhere: Matthew 5:13 to the crowds on the mountain, Luke 14:34–35 to the crowds on the road. Luke 17:1–2 sets the millstone saying among teaching to the disciples.
settings.readers: If they were in Rome under Nero, readers facing persecution and quarrels heard "everyone will be salted with fire" as a word about trial and faithfulness, and "keep peace" as a word to their own divided community.

traditions.q: What was the light the disciples saw on the mountain (9:2–3)?
views: The light of Tabor was the uncreated light of God's own glory, his energies, not a created light: the disciples saw the divinity of Christ shining through his body as far as they could bear. Gregory Palamas defended this teaching against Barlaam of Calabria, and councils at Constantinople (1341–1351) affirmed it. The same light is the goal of prayer and of theosis, union with God.

The transfiguration is a foretaste of Christ's glorious coming and of the glory of the resurrection (Catechism 554–556). Thomas Aquinas taught that the brightness came from the glory of Christ's soul overflowing into his body for a moment, as a preview of the glorified body (Summa Theologiae III, q. 45). Catholic theology has not made the Palamite distinction between God's essence and energies its own, though many Catholic theologians today treat it with respect.

The disciples were given a taste of Christ's heavenly glory to strengthen them before the scandal of the cross; Calvin warns that they did not see his divinity as it is in itself, but only as much as they could bear. No doctrine about the nature of the light is drawn from the passage.
